GWS 3560.d: This course is a survey of historical, cultural, and social aspects of human sexuality. The interplay between sex and society will be the major focus. GWS 3650.d: In this course, students apply the tools of economic analysis to issues affecting marginalized groups (as determined by, for example, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, age, and ability) in the United States. Verification burden is low, since feminist pedagogy requires a human TA to model discussion norms and support students appropriately, keeping close faculty supervision the binding constraint on substitution today.

Over five years, some scaffolding functions of this course, drafting workshop materials, summarizing pedagogical readings, or generating discussion prompts, plausibly see increased AI assistance as capability and adoption both grow, consistent with capability-trend research on expanding task-time horizons and diffusion data indicating adoption is still uneven but rising. However, the course's defining instrumental task is direct human mentorship of peer students inside a feminist pedagogical framework, which depends on real-time relational judgment, modeling classroom norms, and responsiveness to individual students, functions the jagged-frontier finding suggests AI performs unevenly and with miscalibrated confidence outside well-structured domains. Because the training explicitly requires close faculty supervision and prior completion of the course being assisted, institutional oversight of the TA role stays intact. The realistic expectation is incremental tool-assisted preparation work rather than substitution of the supervised teaching-assistant relationship itself.

Projecting a decade forward, sustained capability growth could make AI tutoring and pedagogical-material generation considerably more capable, and GDPval-style benchmarks approaching but not yet matching human-expert performance on realistic deliverables suggest such tools will keep improving without full parity. Whether that capability translates into displacing this course's supervised peer-mentoring role depends heavily on institutional choices about how GWS courses are staffed and how feminist pedagogy is taught, factors not determined by model capability alone. The course's structure, requiring completion of the assisted course with a strong grade and ongoing faculty oversight, anchors it to a specific institutional relationship rather than a portable content-delivery task. Given uneven long-run diffusion evidence and the relational, supervisory core of the role, a confident forecast of substitution by 2036 is unsupported; the more defensible expectation is continued need for trained, supervised human teaching assistants.
GWS 4970.d: This course provides students with an intensive experience as an undergraduate teaching assistant in courses offered through Gender, Women, and Sexualities Studies (GWS) either on campus or online. Under close faculty supervision, this course provides training and support for students to learn about feminist pedagogy and processes involved in teaching gender, women, and sexualities studies courses. Students utilize what they have learned in previous GWS courses to assist other students enrolled in these classes. The experience includes workshop attendance with additional hours of application in the course. Students need to have already taken the course for which they will be serving as a Teacher Assistant.
